title: 1 Corinthians 15:20–28
context: Paul now states the positive truth: Christ has been raised as the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. As death came through one man, so resurrection comes through one man; as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive, each in his own order. Christ reigns until he has put all enemies under his feet, and the last enemy to be destroyed is death. Then the Son himself will be subjected to the Father, so that God may be all in all. Verse 22 is often discussed in debates over the scope of salvation, and verse 28 has a long history in discussions of the Trinity. Arminian and Reformed readers differ over the scope of “all” in verse 22, though both reject universalism.

verses.text: But now Christ has been raised from the dead. He became the first fruits of those who are asleep.
verses.arminianNotes: Christ has been raised as the firstfruits of those who sleep. Arminian readers see the guarantee of the full harvest of believers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the firstfruits belong to and guarantee the harvest. Christ’s resurrection is the pledge that his people will be raised.

verses.text: For since death came by man, the resurrection of the dead also came by man.
verses.arminianNotes: Since death came by a man, the resurrection also came by a man. Arminian readers see Christ’s humanity as essential to his saving work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the federal headship of Adam and Christ, a key theme in covenant theology. Each man acts for those he represents.

verses.text: For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.
verses.arminianNotes: As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. Arminian readers see Christ’s work as broad in scope, offered to all, while only those in Christ by faith share the resurrection to life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see “all in Christ” as those united to him, just as “all in Adam” are those united to Adam. The parallel shows Christ’s headship effectively securing life for his people.
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions reject universalism here. Arminian readers stress a provision that matches Adam’s reach, received by faith. Reformed readers stress two heads, each securing the destiny of those united to him.

verses.text: But each in his own order: Christ the first fruits, then those who are Christ’s, at his coming.
verses.arminianNotes: Each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming. Arminian readers see the resurrection to life for those who are Christ’s.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that “those who are Christ’s” recalls the people given to the Son by the Father in John 6:37–39. The order of resurrection is secure because they belong to him.

verses.text: Then the end comes, when he will deliver up the Kingdom to God, even the Father; when he will have abolished all rule and all authority and power.
verses.arminianNotes: Then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to the Father, having abolished all rule and power. Arminian readers see the final victory of Christ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the consummation of Christ’s mediatorial kingdom, a theme in Reformed eschatology. The Son’s work as mediator reaches its goal when he presents the kingdom to the Father.

verses.text: For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.
verses.arminianNotes: He must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet. Arminian readers see Christ’s present reign moving toward final victory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Psalm 110:1 fulfilled. Christ reigns now, and his reign is certain to prevail over every enemy.

verses.text: The last enemy that will be abolished is death.
verses.arminianNotes: The last enemy to be destroyed is death. Arminian readers see the ultimate defeat of death in Christ’s victory. Death is the final consequence of sin to be undone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that death is an enemy, not a friend. Its destruction completes the reversal of the curse that began with Adam.

verses.text: For, “He put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when he says, “All things are put in subjection”, it is evident that he is excepted who subjected all things to him.
verses.arminianNotes: He has put all things under his feet, except the one who put them under him. Arminian readers see Psalm 8 fulfilled in Christ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Father’s sovereign appointment of all things to the Son. Psalm 8’s vision of human dominion is fulfilled in the last Adam.

verses.text: When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son will also himself be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, that God may be all in all.
verses.arminianNotes: Then the Son will be subjected to the Father, that God may be all in all. Arminian readers see the Son’s subjection as his role as mediator, not a denial of his deity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same. Calvin read the Son’s subjection in terms of his mediatorial office, not his divine nature, which is equal with the Father’s.
